title: Routes II: Lungs, Nose, Eye & Injections
summary: Discover specialized routes, from inhalers and eye drops to long-acting injections and implanted pumps.

lessons.title: Pulmonary Delivery: MDIs, DPIs, Nebulizers and Aerosol Deposition

levels.kid:
Your lungs are like an upside-down tree. The big trunk is your windpipe, and it splits into smaller and smaller branches. At the very ends are tiny balloons where air goes into your blood.

Some medicines work best when you breathe them in. That way they go straight to the lungs, where the problem is. People with asthma use a puffer called an **inhaler**.

But there is a trick. The medicine has to be made into super tiny drops or specks. Big specks crash into the back of your throat, like a ball hitting a wall. Very tiny ones can travel deep into the branches.

That is why doctors teach people to breathe in the right way when they use an inhaler.
levels.hs:
**Pulmonary delivery** means giving a drug by inhalation so it lands in the airways or lungs. It is ideal for lung diseases like **asthma** and **COPD** (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). The drug acts right where it is needed, it often works within minutes, and much less of it reaches the rest of the body, so there are fewer side effects.

The drug must be made into an **aerosol**: tiny liquid droplets or solid particles floating in air. Size matters most. Scientists measure **aerodynamic diameter** in micrometres (µm):
- Larger than about 5 µm: particles hit the throat and get swallowed.
- About 1-5 µm: the ideal size to reach the airways and lungs.
- Smaller than about 1 µm: many are simply breathed back out.

There are three main devices:
- **Metered-dose inhaler (MDI)**: a pressurized canister that sprays a measured puff using a propellant gas.
- **Dry powder inhaler (DPI)**: the patient's own fast, deep breath pulls a fine powder out of the device.
- **Nebulizer**: a machine turns a liquid into a mist that is breathed in over several minutes. It is useful for small children or very sick patients.

A real example: **salbutamol** (called albuterol in the US) from an MDI relaxes tightened airway muscle within minutes during an asthma attack. A **spacer**, a tube attached to the MDI, makes it much easier to time the puff with the breath.
levels.college:
The lung offers a huge absorptive surface, roughly 100 m² of alveoli. Its epithelium is very thin (about 0.1-0.2 µm at the alveolus), and drugs absorbed there skip first-pass liver metabolism. For airway disease the main goal is a high local concentration with low systemic exposure, which gives a strong **therapeutic index** advantage over oral dosing.

**Deposition mechanisms** depend on particle size, airflow and breathing pattern:
- **Inertial impaction**: large or fast particles cannot follow bends in the airway and hit the oropharynx and large airways. This dominates above about 5 µm.
- **Gravitational sedimentation**: particles of 1-5 µm settle in the small airways and alveoli. Breath-holding helps by giving them time to settle.
- **Diffusion (Brownian motion)**: matters below about 0.5 µm, in the deep lung.

Aerosols are described by **mass median aerodynamic diameter (MMAD)** and **geometric standard deviation**. The **fine particle fraction** is the share below about 5 µm. These values are measured with cascade impactors such as the Andersen cascade impactor or the Next Generation Impactor (NGI).

**Devices:**
- **pMDI**: the drug is dissolved or suspended in a hydrofluoroalkane (HFA) propellant. A metering valve delivers each puff. CFC propellants were phased out under the Montreal Protocol. A fast-moving plume means the patient must coordinate pressing and breathing in. Spacers and valved holding chambers slow the plume and cut throat deposition.
- **DPI**: micronized drug is usually blended with coarse lactose carrier particles. The patient's inspiratory effort disperses the powder. No coordination is needed, but there must be enough inspiratory flow.
- **Nebulizers**: jet (compressed air), ultrasonic, or vibrating mesh types. They need little skill but take minutes per use. **Soft mist inhalers** (Respimat) make a slow, long-lasting mist.

Even with good technique, often only about 10-40% of the emitted drug reaches the lungs. Most of the rest is swallowed.
levels.phd:
Regional deposition follows from particle dynamics in a branching network of about 23 generations, as in the classic Weibel lung model. The **Stokes number** (Stk = ρd²U/18μD) predicts impaction. Because it scales with the square of particle diameter and with velocity, the impaction parameter ρd²Q is a useful predictor of oropharyngeal loss. This explains why fast inhalation helps a DPI disperse its powder yet also increases throat deposition. Sedimentation probability rises with residence time, which is why breath-holding of about 10 s is recommended. The ICRP (1994) and Heyder et al. deposition curves show a deposition minimum near 0.3-0.5 µm. Below that size diffusion takes over, and above it impaction and sedimentation do.

**Formulation physics.**
- In HFA pMDIs, solution formulations such as beclometasone in HFA-134a with ethanol give extra-fine aerosols (MMAD near 1 µm). These reach more of the small airways, so the doses are re-labelled relative to CFC products.
- Suspension MDIs need physical stability against creaming and flocculation.
- In DPIs, **cohesive and adhesive balance** is key. Micronized drug (under 5 µm) is very cohesive. Carrier lactose, fine lactose and force-control agents such as magnesium stearate change how easily drug detaches during inhalation.
- Engineered particles avoid carriers altogether. Examples are PulmoSphere porous particles (tobramycin inhalation powder), spray-dried large porous particles (Edwards and Langer, 1997) and Technosphere (inhaled insulin, Afrezza). Large geometric size with low density gives a small aerodynamic diameter but less aggregation and less macrophage uptake.

**Fate after deposition.** Particles that land in the conducting airways are cleared by the **mucociliary escalator** within hours. Insoluble particles in the alveoli face **alveolar macrophages**. Lipophilic small molecules are absorbed within minutes. Lung retention can be extended by slow dissolution, as with fluticasone propionate, or by trapping inside cells, as with lipophilic amines like salmeterol. Systemic exposure equals lung absorption plus the swallowed fraction minus oral first-pass loss. Corticosteroids such as ciclesonide (a prodrug) and fluticasone are designed to have low oral bioavailability.

There is a controversy over the **small-airway hypothesis**. It is still disputed whether extra-fine aerosols improve outcomes in asthma, beyond what they do to imaging and deposition scores.
levels.expert:
Clinically, **device technique is the main failure point**. Studies repeatedly find critical errors in a large share of inhaler users. Common errors include failing to breathe out before inhaling, poor timing of the pMDI puff with the breath, and too little or too slow inspiratory effort with a DPI. Prescribe a device the patient can actually use, check technique at every visit, and avoid mixing device types. **Peak inspiratory flow** against device resistance can be measured with an In-Check dial. Elderly patients, those with severe COPD, and patients during an exacerbation may not generate enough flow for high-resistance DPIs, and a pMDI with a spacer or a nebulizer may suit them better. In acute severe asthma, a pMDI with a spacer works as well as a nebulizer in many trials.

**Regulatory and bioequivalence complexity.** Generic orally inhaled products require a weight-of-evidence approach. This combines in vitro equivalence (delivered dose uniformity and APSD by NGI), pharmacokinetic studies (which mostly reflect lung deposition when charcoal blocks absorption from the gut), and pharmacodynamic or clinical endpoint studies. Device similarity also matters. This is why generic Advair (fluticasone/salmeterol) took many years to arrive.

**Current developments.**
- **Low-global-warming propellants**. HFA-134a and HFA-227ea are potent greenhouse gases. Reformulation with HFA-152a and HFO-1234ze is under way under the Kigali Amendment and EU F-gas rules. Bridging studies are needed because these propellants have different solvent and plume properties.
- **Inhaled antimicrobials for cystic fibrosis**, such as tobramycin, aztreonam lysine, and amikacin liposome for MAC lung disease. They reach high airway concentrations but can cause bronchospasm.
- **Inhaled systemic drugs** take advantage of rapid absorption. Examples are Afrezza insulin, inhaled loxapine (Adasuve, which carries a bronchospasm warning), and levodopa powder (Inbrija) for Parkinson's OFF episodes.
- **Smart inhalers** with adherence sensors, and inhaled biologics or mRNA. The open problems for these are protein instability during aerosolization, immunogenicity and macrophage clearance.

There are still **open questions**. Patient-specific airway geometry and disease such as mucus plugging make deposition unpredictable, and in vitro-in vivo correlation using realistic mouth-throat models such as the Alberta idealized throat is still imperfect. Long-term safety of chronic lung exposure to new excipients also remains a regulatory concern.

keyPoints: Inhaled drugs act locally in the lungs with fast onset and low systemic exposure
Particles of about 1-5 µm aerodynamic diameter reach the airways best
Impaction (large), sedimentation (1-5 µm) and diffusion (tiny) govern deposition
pMDIs need coordination; spacers reduce throat deposition
DPIs rely on the patient's inspiratory flow to disperse powder
Nebulizers need little skill; poor technique is the commonest cause of treatment failure

test.q: Which aerodynamic size range deposits best in the airways and lungs?
choices: About 10-20 µm
About 1-5 µm
About 0.01-0.1 µm
About 50-100 µm
test.explain: Particles of about 1-5 µm avoid throat impaction but are big enough to settle. Particles that are much smaller tend to be breathed out.

test.q: Large particles inhaled quickly mostly deposit in the throat by which mechanism?
choices: Mucociliary clearance
Brownian diffusion
Gravitational sedimentation
Inertial impaction
test.explain: Fast, large particles cannot follow the bends of the airway, so they hit the oropharynx. Sedimentation affects smaller, slower particles.

test.q: What disperses the powder in a dry powder inhaler?
choices: A vibrating mesh membrane
Compressed air from a pump
The patient's inspiratory airflow
A pressurized propellant gas
test.explain: DPIs are breath-actuated, so the patient's own fast inhalation breaks up and carries the powder.

test.q: Why is a spacer attached to a pressurized metered-dose inhaler?
choices: It adds lactose carrier to the drug
It turns the spray into a dry powder
It slows the plume and reduces throat deposition
It heats the drug so it dissolves faster
test.explain: A spacer slows the fast plume and removes the need for exact timing. This cuts throat impaction and improves lung delivery.

test.q: Why is breath-holding after inhalation recommended?
choices: It pushes particles into the stomach
It activates the propellant gas
It gives particles time to settle
It raises the speed of airflow
test.explain: Sedimentation increases with residence time, so holding the breath lets 1-5 µm particles settle in the lungs.

test.q: Which propellant class replaced CFCs in metered-dose inhalers?
choices: Hydrofluoroalkanes
Butane blends
Liquid nitrogen
Nitrous oxides
test.explain: HFA propellants such as HFA-134a replaced CFCs after the Montreal Protocol phase-out.

test.q: A key advantage of inhaled asthma drugs over oral tablets is:
choices: Local action with fewer systemic effects
No need for any patient technique
Higher drug levels in the whole body
Slower onset that lasts for weeks
test.explain: Inhalation puts drug where it is needed, which improves the therapeutic index. Technique still matters a great deal.

test.q: Which device is often chosen for very young children or very sick patients?
choices: Transdermal patch
Dry powder inhaler
Nebulizer
Chewable tablet
test.explain: Nebulizers need only normal tidal breathing, so they suit patients who cannot coordinate or inhale forcefully.

test.q: What is the usual fate of most inhaled drug that does not reach the lungs?
choices: It is absorbed through the skin
It stays in the device chamber
It is breathed out at once
It is swallowed into the gut
test.explain: Drug that hits the mouth and throat is swallowed. Only about 10-40% of the emitted dose typically reaches the lungs.

test.q: Particles in the conducting airways are cleared by the mucociliary ___.
test.explain: Beating cilia move mucus and trapped particles upward toward the throat within hours.

test.q: What does the abbreviation DPI stand for?
test.explain: A DPI delivers micronized powder dispersed by the patient's breath.

test.q: Coarse ___ carrier particles are commonly blended with micronized drug in DPIs.
test.explain: Lactose carriers improve how the powder flows and is metered. The drug detaches from them during inhalation.

kidTest.q: What does an inhaler do?
choices: Sends medicine into the lungs
Cleans dirt from your teeth
Measures how tall you are
kidTest.explain: You breathe the medicine straight into your lungs.

kidTest.q: What happens to big medicine specks?
choices: They crash into the throat
They turn into tiny bubbles
They reach the tiny balloons
kidTest.explain: Big specks hit the back of the throat, like a ball hitting a wall.

kidTest.q: Which illness is often treated with an inhaler?
choices: A broken arm
A sore toe
Asthma
kidTest.explain: Inhalers help people with asthma breathe more easily.

kidTest.q: Why do people learn how to breathe with an inhaler?
choices: So the medicine reaches deep inside
So the medicine tastes much sweeter
So the inhaler makes a loud sound
kidTest.explain: Breathing the right way helps the medicine travel deep into the lungs.

kidTest.q: Your lungs look like an upside-down t _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The windpipe is like a trunk that splits into smaller and smaller branches.

advancedTest.q: A COPD patient with weak inspiratory flow gets poor results from a high-resistance DPI. What is the best reasoning-based switch?
choices: A different DPI with a higher resistance design
Inhaling more slowly through the same DPI device
An extra-fine powder in the same type of DPI
A pMDI used with a spacer or a nebulizer
advancedTest.explain: DPIs depend on the patient's own flow to disperse powder. A pMDI with a spacer or a nebulizer does not need forceful inhalation.

advancedTest.q: Since the impaction parameter scales as ρd²Q, what effect does a faster inhalation through a DPI have?
choices: No change in where particles deposit
Better dispersion but more oropharyngeal loss
More alveolar diffusion of large particles
Less dispersion and less throat deposition
advancedTest.explain: Higher flow breaks up the powder more effectively but raises impaction in the throat, which is the classic DPI trade-off.

advancedTest.q: Why are porous particles with large geometric size and low density useful for deep-lung delivery?
choices: Their large mass gives them strong impaction in the deep lung
Low aerodynamic diameter but less clumping and phagocytosis
Their high density speeds up sedimentation in the alveoli
They dissolve fully in the propellant before they are released
advancedTest.explain: Low density reduces aerodynamic diameter while the large geometric size limits aggregation and phagocytosis by macrophages.

advancedTest.q: Why are pharmacokinetic studies of inhaled generics done with oral charcoal blockade?
choices: To prevent mucociliary clearance in the lung
To increase gut absorption of the drug
To slow dissolution of particles in mucus
So plasma levels mainly reflect lung deposition
advancedTest.explain: Charcoal blocks absorption of the swallowed fraction, so systemic exposure reports mainly on how much drug reached the lungs.

lessons.title: Nasal Delivery and the Nose-to-Brain Pathway

levels.kid:
Your nose isn't just for smelling. Doctors can use it to give medicine too! When you spray medicine up your nose, it lands on a thin, wet lining full of tiny blood vessels, so it soaks in fast, like water into a paper towel. Some medicine can even sneak along special nerves at the very top of your nose that connect almost straight to your brain, skipping the long trip through your stomach.

That's why nose sprays can work in minutes instead of hours. Doctors use this trick to stop bad migraine headaches quickly. A spray called naloxone can also help, fast, a person whose breathing has slowed dangerously because of strong opioid medicines.
levels.hs:
The inside of your nose is lined with a thin, richly vascularized mucosa that can absorb medicine quickly, partly because it skips the **first-pass metabolism** that pills undergo in the liver after swallowing. Most of the nasal cavity is covered by **respiratory epithelium**, where sprayed drug diffuses into capillaries and reaches the bloodstream within minutes.

A small patch at the top of the nasal cavity, the **olfactory epithelium**, contains nerve endings that connect directly to the brain's olfactory bulb. This creates a possible "nose-to-brain" shortcut: drug molecules can travel along olfactory and **trigeminal nerve** pathways, partly bypassing the **blood-brain barrier**, which normally blocks many drugs from entering brain tissue.

Real examples: sumatriptan and zolmitriptan nasal sprays treat migraine attacks quickly; naloxone nasal spray reverses life-threatening opioid toxicity within minutes without an injection; esketamine nasal spray treats severe depression, relying partly on this nose-to-brain route.

Challenges limit how well this works: **mucociliary clearance** sweeps mucus (and drug) toward the throat within about 15-20 minutes, enzymes in the nasal lining break down some drugs, and the olfactory region is small, so only a limited amount of drug can take the direct brain route.
levels.college:
Nasal mucosa has two functionally distinct zones:
- **Respiratory epithelium** (roughly 90-95% of surface area): ciliated, pseudostratified columnar cells sitting over a dense capillary bed. Drug diffuses across (paracellular and transcellular routes) into systemic circulation, avoiding hepatic first-pass metabolism, giving rapid Tmax for small, moderately lipophilic molecules.
- **Olfactory epithelium** (roughly 3-10% of surface, on the upper septum and superior turbinate): home to olfactory sensory neurons whose axons pass through the cribriform plate into the olfactory bulb.

**Nose-to-brain routes**, both partly bypassing the blood-brain barrier:
- Olfactory pathway: drug crosses the epithelium and moves along or around olfactory neurons into the olfactory bulb, then diffuses into CSF or brain tissue.
- Trigeminal pathway: ophthalmic and maxillary branches innervating the nasal mucosa terminate in the brainstem, offering access to more caudal brain regions.

**Limiting factors**: mucociliary clearance removes much of a dose within 15-20 minutes; nasal peptidases and cytochrome P450 enzymes degrade peptides and some small molecules; the small olfactory surface area restricts how much drug reaches the brain directly; larger or hydrophilic molecules cross poorly without help.

**Formulation strategies**: mucoadhesive polymers (chitosan, carbopol) prolong mucosal contact time; permeation enhancers (cyclodextrins, surfactants) loosen tight junctions; devices can be engineered to deposit droplets on the upper nasal cavity rather than the anterior nasal valve, where most conventional spray lands and is quickly cleared.

**Approved CNS-related nasal products** include esketamine for treatment-resistant depression, sumatriptan and zolmitriptan for migraine, diazepam for seizure clusters, and naloxone for reversing opioid toxicity, though much of their fast action likely reflects rapid systemic absorption as much as any direct brain route.
levels.phd:
William Frey's 1989 hypothesis proposed a direct nose-to-brain pathway, based on rodent experiments showing labeled tracers and peptides (e.g., wheat germ agglutinin-HRP, insulin-like growth factor) appearing in CSF and olfactory bulb at concentrations exceeding predictions from systemic blood-brain barrier crossing.

Two cellular-level sub-routes are described: **intracellular axonal transport**, in which olfactory sensory neurons endocytose drug and carry it anterograde along axons to the bulb over hours to days (documented for some tracers and neurotropic viruses); and **extracellular/paracellular transport**, diffusion through perineural and perivascular clefts surrounding olfactory and trigeminal nerve bundles, which can deliver molecules to CSF within minutes and is considered the dominant route for rapid pharmacologic effects.

Rodent microdialysis studies comparing CSF-to-plasma ratios after intranasal versus intravenous administration show several-fold greater brain exposure via the intranasal route for peptides that poorly cross the BBB systemically (insulin, oxytocin), supporting a non-systemic contribution for at least part of the administered drug.

**Controversy**: translating this to humans is contested because olfactory epithelium occupies only ~3-10% of human nasal surface area versus up to ~50% in rodents, raising doubt about whether rodent data scale. Human trials of intranasal oxytocin and insulin show measurable behavioral and cognitive effects, but direct human CSF sampling rarely confirms a dominant non-systemic route; observed effects could partly reflect peripheral signaling (e.g., vagal) rather than true direct transport.

**Efflux and metabolism**: P-glycoprotein and CYP3A expressed in nasal mucosa limit net flux of substrates; aminopeptidases degrade therapeutic peptides, motivating enzyme-resistant analog design. Desmopressin's D-amino acid substitution is a classic example of structural modification to resist nasal peptidase degradation.

Receptor-mediated transcytosis strategies, using transferrin-receptor-targeted nanocarriers given intranasally, are being explored to combine olfactory bypass with enhanced parenchymal penetration, though clinical validation remains limited.
levels.expert:
Device engineering has become central to exploiting this route clinically. **Precision Olfactory Delivery (POD)** platforms use a propellant-driven plume aimed at the superior and posterior nasal cavity to maximize deposition on olfactory epithelium, since over 80% of a conventional spray lands on the anterior nasal valve and is cleared before reaching useful tissue. Trudhesa, a dihydroergotamine nasal spray approved in 2021 for acute migraine, uses this approach to reach the upper nasal cavity reliably regardless of head position.

Nasal vaccines illustrate a related but distinct use of nasal anatomy: the live attenuated influenza vaccine (FluMist) and newer intranasal COVID-19 candidates target **nasal-associated lymphoid tissue (NALT)** to generate mucosal IgA at the site of respiratory viral entry, rather than aiming for CNS delivery.

A notable safety pitfall: intranasal zinc gluconate cold remedies (marketed as Zicam) caused cases of permanent anosmia by damaging olfactory sensory neurons, prompting an FDA warning in 2009. This is a reminder that targeting the olfactory region for therapeutic benefit also exposes a uniquely vulnerable neural tissue to potential irritant injury.

Proving genuine direct nose-to-brain transport in humans remains methodologically difficult, since any CNS effect after nasal administration could equally arise from systemic absorption and ordinary blood-brain barrier crossing. Research approaches include PET imaging with radiolabeled drug, rare direct CSF sampling, and experimental designs that pharmacologically restrict systemic nasal absorption (e.g., with vasoconstrictors) to isolate a purely local, non-vascular contribution.

Open questions include how reliably olfactory-targeted deposition can be achieved across variable individual nasal anatomy, the long-term safety of chronic permeation-enhancer use, and whether intranasal biologic or nanoparticle carriers can produce clinically meaningful effects in neurodegenerative disease. Intranasal insulin trials for mild cognitive impairment and oxytocin trials in autism show mechanistic promise but inconsistent clinical effect sizes so far.

keyPoints: Nasal mucosa's dense vasculature allows rapid drug absorption while skipping first-pass liver metabolism
Respiratory epithelium absorbs drug into the bloodstream; olfactory epithelium offers a possible route into the brain
The nose-to-brain pathway uses olfactory and trigeminal nerve routes to partly bypass the blood-brain barrier
Mucociliary clearance and nasal enzymes limit how much drug is absorbed or reaches the brain
Approved nasal CNS drugs include esketamine, sumatriptan/zolmitriptan, naloxone, and dihydroergotamine
Direct human nose-to-brain transport is hard to prove and remains scientifically debated

test.q: Why can drugs absorbed through the nose act especially fast?
choices: It skips first-pass metabolism in the liver
It is more potent chemically
It is sterilized before administration
It dissolves slower than stomach acid
test.explain: Nasal absorption sends drug straight into the bloodstream via mucosal capillaries, bypassing the liver's first-pass metabolism that oral pills must go through.

test.q: Which part of the nasal cavity contains nerve endings that connect directly to the brain's olfactory bulb?
choices: Olfactory epithelium
Nasal septum
Respiratory epithelium
Nasal vestibule
test.explain: The olfactory epithelium, though small, houses sensory neurons whose axons run into the olfactory bulb, offering a possible brain-access route.

test.q: Besides the olfactory nerve, which nerve can carry nasally applied drug toward the brainstem?
choices: Vagus nerve, which innervates throat and visceral organs
Trigeminal nerve, which innervates the nasal mucosa
Optic nerve, which carries visual signals from the retina
Facial nerve, which controls muscles of facial expression
test.explain: The trigeminal nerve's ophthalmic and maxillary branches innervate the nasal mucosa and terminate in the brainstem.

test.q: Mucociliary clearance moves nasal spray toward the throat within about:
choices: 2-3 minutes
2-3 hours
24 hours
15-20 minutes
test.explain: Cilia sweep mucus, and any undissolved drug, toward the throat within roughly 15-20 minutes, limiting absorption time.

test.q: Which nasal spray is used for rapid reversal of life-threatening opioid toxicity?
choices: Zolmitriptan
Desmopressin
Esketamine
Naloxone
test.explain: Naloxone nasal spray reverses opioid toxicity within minutes without requiring an injection.

test.q: Esketamine nasal spray is approved to treat:
choices: Recurrent seizure clusters at home
Treatment-resistant depression
Opioid toxicity emergencies
Acute migraine headache attacks
test.explain: Esketamine nasal spray treats treatment-resistant depression, partly relying on the nose-to-brain route.

test.q: What is a key purpose of mucoadhesive polymers like chitosan in nasal formulations?
choices: Prolong drug contact with the mucosa
Sterilize the nasal cavity lining
Increase mucus production long-term
Numb nasal nerve endings for comfort
test.explain: Mucoadhesive polymers keep the formulation in contact with the mucosa longer, giving more time for absorption before mucociliary clearance removes it.

test.q: Sumatriptan and zolmitriptan nasal sprays are primarily used to treat:
choices: Seasonal allergies
Nasal congestion
Migraine attacks
Bacterial sinus infections
test.explain: Both are triptans delivered nasally for fast relief of migraine attacks.

test.q: What generally limits the absorption of large peptide drugs given nasally?
choices: A melting point too high for body temperature
Nasal enzymes and poor mucosal permeability
Excess binding to circulating red blood cells
Rapid destruction by gastric acid after spraying
test.explain: Nasal peptidases break down peptides, and their size limits how well they cross the mucosal barrier, unlike small lipophilic drugs.

test.q: What barrier normally blocks many drugs from entering brain tissue from the blood, which the nose-to-brain route can partly bypass?
test.explain: The blood-brain barrier restricts drug entry from blood into brain tissue; olfactory and trigeminal pathways offer a partial bypass.

test.q: Nasal drugs enter the bloodstream directly, so they avoid ___-pass metabolism by the liver.
test.explain: Oral pills are processed by the liver before reaching circulation (first-pass metabolism); nasal absorption skips this step.

test.q: The region of the nasal cavity responsible for the sense of smell and potential brain access is called the ___ epithelium.
test.explain: The olfactory epithelium, located in the upper nasal cavity, contains neurons connecting to the olfactory bulb.

kidTest.q: What can nose sprays reach quickly that pills take longer to reach?
choices: the hair
the toenails
the brain
kidTest.explain: Some medicine can travel along nerves near the top of the nose straight toward the brain.

kidTest.q: Why do nose sprays work fast?
choices: the nose is far away from the brain
the inside of the nose is very cold
it has lots of tiny blood vessels
kidTest.explain: The nose's lining is full of tiny blood vessels that soak up medicine quickly.

kidTest.q: What sweeps medicine away from inside your nose after a while?
choices: your teeth when you chew
tiny hairs called cilia
your eyelashes when you blink
kidTest.explain: Tiny hairs called cilia sweep mucus, and medicine, toward your throat over time.

kidTest.q: Which medicine can quickly help someone whose breathing slowed from strong opioid medicine?
choices: a daily vitamin C tablet
antibiotic eye drops
naloxone nose spray
kidTest.explain: Naloxone nose spray can quickly help a person whose breathing has slowed dangerously from opioids.

kidTest.q: What is the name of the special nerve pathway at the top of the nose that connects toward the brain? Hint: o _ _ _ _ _ _ _ y
kidTest.explain: The olfactory pathway runs from nerve endings in the nose into the brain's olfactory bulb.

advancedTest.q: Why might rodent studies overestimate direct nose-to-brain drug transport relative to humans?
choices: Human trigeminal nerve fibers do not innervate nasal mucosa
Rodent olfactory epithelium contains far fewer sensory neurons than human epithelium
Rodent nasal mucosa lacks mucociliary clearance mechanisms
Olfactory epithelium covers a much larger nasal surface fraction in rodents than humans
advancedTest.explain: Rodents have olfactory epithelium covering up to ~50% of nasal surface versus only ~3-10% in humans, so direct transport findings may not scale to people.

advancedTest.q: Which pathway is thought to produce the most rapid (minutes-scale) appearance of nasally applied drug in CSF?
choices: Extracellular flow along perineural and perivascular clefts
Active transport across red blood cell membranes in capillaries
Intracellular axonal transport along olfactory neurons
Uptake into blood and transport via the hepatic portal vein
advancedTest.explain: Extracellular diffusion along perineural and perivascular clefts can move drug into CSF within minutes, unlike the slower (hours-to-days) intracellular axonal route.

advancedTest.q: What is a key methodological challenge in proving direct nose-to-brain transport in human trials?
choices: The rarity of direct CSF sampling in human intranasal drug trials
The near absence of noticeable CNS effects after intranasal dosing in humans
The limited accessibility of human olfactory epithelium to any drug formulation
The difficulty of separating direct nasal transport effects from systemic absorption effects
advancedTest.explain: Any CNS effect after intranasal administration could arise from ordinary systemic absorption crossing the blood-brain barrier, making it hard to isolate a true direct pathway without specialized study designs.

advancedTest.q: Why did intranasal zinc gluconate cold remedies raise a safety concern distinct from typical oral cold medicines?
choices: They caused permanent loss of smell by damaging olfactory epithelium
They were absorbed too slowly to produce any effect
They caused the same liver toxicity seen with oral acetaminophen poisoning
They triggered first-pass metabolism complications unique to the nose
advancedTest.explain: Intranasal zinc gluconate products damaged olfactory sensory neurons, causing permanent anosmia in some users, a risk specific to targeting the olfactory region.

lessons.title: Ophthalmic Delivery: Drops, Inserts and Intravitreal Injection

levels.kid:
Your eye is a tricky place to send medicine, because it is built to keep things out! Every time you blink, tears wash the front of your eye, like windshield wipers on a rainy car.

One eye drop is bigger than your eye can hold. Some spills onto your cheek, and lots of it drains down a tiny tube into your nose. That's why some people taste their eye drops!

Eye medicines must be **sterile**, which means super clean with no germs at all. Scientists also invent clever helpers:
- Thick, gel-like drops that stay put longer.
- Tiny soft inserts that let medicine out slowly, like a tea bag.
- For the very back of the eye, an eye doctor can use a very thin needle to place medicine right inside. The eye is numbed first, so it is quick and gentle.
levels.hs:
**Ophthalmic delivery** means getting medicine into the eye. The eye has two zones: the **anterior segment** (the front: cornea, iris, lens) and the **posterior segment** (the back: the jelly-like vitreous and the retina). Different methods reach different zones.

**Eye drops** treat the front of the eye, but they are surprisingly wasteful. A typical drop is about 30-50 microliters, while the tear film holds only about 7-10. The extra spills over, and blinking plus tear flow drain the rest through the **nasolacrimal duct** into the nose within minutes. Often less than 5% of the drug gets through the **cornea**, the clear window at the front of the eye.

Drained drug can enter the bloodstream through the lining of the nose. Example: **timolol**, a beta-blocker drop for glaucoma, can slow the heart or trigger asthma, because it skips first-pass metabolism in the liver. Pressing gently on the inner corner of the eye (**punctal occlusion**) and closing the eyes for a couple of minutes reduces this.

Ways to do better:
- Thicker drops, gels and ointments stay on the eye longer.
- **Inserts** and **punctal plugs** release drug slowly.
- Eye products must be **sterile**; multi-use bottles contain **preservatives** such as benzalkonium chloride.

Drops barely reach the retina. For diseases like wet macular degeneration, doctors give **intravitreal injections** of drugs such as aflibercept directly into the vitreous.
levels.college:
**Barriers at the front.** A topical drug must cross the **cornea**, a three-layer sandwich:
- **Epithelium**: lipophilic, sealed by tight junctions; the main barrier to hydrophilic drugs.
- **Stroma**: about 90% of corneal thickness, watery collagen; a barrier to very lipophilic drugs.
- **Endothelium**: a leaky single layer facing the aqueous humor.
The best corneal penetrants are small with balanced lipophilicity. The un-ionized form crosses the epithelium more easily, so pH and pKa matter. Large hydrophilic molecules may instead take the **non-corneal route** through conjunctiva and sclera.

**Precorneal loss.** Instilled volume exceeds cul-de-sac capacity, tear turnover runs roughly 1 µL/min (far higher with reflex tearing), and drainage clears most drug within minutes. Formulation counters:
- **Viscosity enhancers** (hypromellose, carbomer) and ointments.
- **In-situ gels**: gellan gum gels with tear cations (Timoptic-XE); poloxamers gel at eye temperature.
- **Prodrugs**: latanoprost is an isopropyl ester hydrolyzed by corneal esterases to its active acid.
- **Suspensions and emulsions** (prednisolone acetate, cyclosporine emulsion) for poorly soluble drugs.
Drops should be near tear pH (~7.4) and isotonic; stinging triggers reflex tearing that washes drug away.

**Preservatives.** Multidose bottles need antimicrobials. **Benzalkonium chloride (BAK)** damages surface epithelium with chronic use, driving preservative-free unit-dose vials and filtered multidose bottles.

**Inserts and implants.** Ocusert (1974) released pilocarpine at near zero order for a week through a rate-controlling membrane. Modern examples: Dextenza (dexamethasone intracanalicular insert, up to 30 days) and the intracameral glaucoma implants Durysta (bimatoprost) and iDose TR (travoprost).

**Back of the eye.** The **blood-retinal barrier** (retinal capillary endothelium plus the **retinal pigment epithelium**, RPE) limits systemic delivery, and drops barely reach the retina. **Intravitreal injection** through the pars plana places drug directly in the vitreous: anti-VEGF biologics (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab, faricimab) for wet AMD and diabetic macular edema, and steroid implants such as **Ozurdex** (dexamethasone in biodegradable PLGA) and **Iluvien** (fluocinolone, non-biodegradable).
levels.phd:
Ocular pharmacokinetics is a race between slow membrane permeation and fast compartmental clearance.

**Precorneal kinetics.** Classic rabbit studies by Robinson and colleagues showed that drainage rate rises with instilled volume, so smaller drops are proportionally more efficient. Corneal absorption is a first-order process competing with drainage, conjunctival uptake and other nonproductive loss; precorneal half-life is only minutes, so bioavailability to aqueous humor typically lands around 1-5%. A large fraction, by some estimates up to ~80%, reaches the systemic circulation via nasal mucosa, bypassing hepatic first pass, which explains clinically significant beta-blockade from timolol drops.

**Corneal permeation as series resistance.** The epithelium acts as a lipid barrier in which permeability rises with log P to a parabolic optimum (roughly log P 2-3), while the hydrated stroma penalizes highly lipophilic solutes. Tight junctions restrict paracellular flux to small solutes, so antibodies are largely excluded. Epithelial esterases are exploited by prodrugs: latanoprost today and, historically, dipivefrin, an epinephrine prodrug.

**Vitreous kinetics.** The human vitreous (~4 mL) is a collagen-hyaluronan gel through which most molecules diffuse fairly freely. Elimination follows two routes: an **anterior route** via aqueous humor turnover, dominant for large hydrophilic molecules, and a **posterior route** across retina and RPE, available to small lipophilic or actively transported drugs. Vitreous half-life therefore generally increases with hydrodynamic size. Small molecules clear in hours, while human aqueous-sampling studies put ranibizumab (a ~48 kDa Fab) at roughly a week, with full-length IgG bevacizumab somewhat longer. Fragment design trades residence time for molar concentration: brolucizumab (~26 kDa scFv) packs more binding sites into the same injection volume.

**Pivotal trials.** MARINA and ANCHOR (2006) established monthly ranibizumab for neovascular AMD. CATT (2011) found off-label bevacizumab noninferior for visual acuity, igniting a lasting cost controversy.

**Implant release mechanics.** Ozurdex relies on PLGA hydrolysis and erosion, producing an initial burst followed by decline over months. Iluvien and the surgically sutured Retisert use non-erodible matrix or reservoir designs that give near-zero-order fluocinolone release over years. The tradeoff is cataract and intraocular pressure elevation inherent to prolonged steroid exposure.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the weakest link in ophthalmic delivery is often the human, not the formulation.

**Topical pitfalls.** Glaucoma adherence studies repeatedly show large gaps between prescribed and actual use, worsened by poor technique: missed eyes, bottle-tip contamination, extra drops. Spacing different drops several minutes apart stops the second from washing out the first. Chronic BAK exposure contributes to ocular surface disease and may lower the success of later glaucoma surgery, an argument for preservative-free regimens and for implants that take the patient out of the loop. Drug-eluting contact lenses (Acuvue Theravision with ketotifen) are an early commercial step.

**Intravitreal practice.** Treat-and-extend regimens titrate intervals to disease activity. Faricimab, blocking both VEGF-A and angiopoietin-2, lets many patients reach 16-week intervals. Safety issues:
- **Endophthalmitis** occurs in roughly 1 in 2,000-5,000 injections; clusters have followed contaminated compounded, repackaged bevacizumab.
- **Brolucizumab** was linked to retinal vasculitis and occlusive vasculopathy tied to anti-drug immune responses, curbing its use.
- Silicone-oil microdroplets from lubricated syringes can cause floaters.
- Systemic exposure differs: bevacizumab's Fc region enables FcRn recycling and prolonged plasma VEGF suppression, while the Fab ranibizumab clears quickly. Cardiovascular relevance remains debated.

**Device lessons.** The refillable Port Delivery System with ranibizumab (Susvimo, approved 2021) was recalled in 2022 over septum dislodgement and returned in 2024. Device engineering, not the drug, limited the platform.

**New routes and modalities.**
- **Suprachoroidal** microinjection (Xipere, triamcinolone for uveitic macular edema) spreads drug circumferentially over choroid and retina with less anterior exposure.
- **Subretinal** AAV gene therapy: voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna, 2017) for RPE65 retinopathy.
- Intravitreal complement inhibitors pegcetacoplan and avacincaptad pegol (2023) for geographic atrophy.
- Encapsulated cells secreting ciliary neurotrophic factor (revakinagene taroretcel, 2025) for macular telangiectasia type 2.
- Tyrosine kinase inhibitor depots (vorolanib, axitinib) in trials aim for roughly six-month treatment intervals.

**Open questions.** Rabbits have smaller vitreous volume, rarer blinking and different clearance, complicating translation. Biosimilar ranibizumab and aflibercept are reshaping access and cost.

keyPoints: Eye drops overflow the tear film; often under 5% crosses the cornea
Nasolacrimal drainage causes systemic effects, as with timolol
Corneal epithelium and stroma favor small drugs of balanced lipophilicity
Gels, prodrugs, inserts and implants extend contact or release
The blood-retinal barrier makes intravitreal delivery key for retinal disease
Anti-VEGF biologics and steroid implants transformed AMD and macular edema care

test.q: Why is most of a standard eye drop wasted?
choices: Eye drops evaporate within a few seconds
The cornea chemically destroys most drugs
Drop volume exceeds what the tear film holds
Light exposure breaks the drug down quickly
test.explain: A drop of about 30-50 microliters is far more than the tear film's 7-10, so the excess spills over and drains away within minutes.

test.q: Where does most of an eye drop drain after instillation?
choices: Into the vitreous gel
Across the lens into the retina
Into the optic nerve sheath
Through the nasolacrimal duct
test.explain: Blinking and tear flow push excess drug through the nasolacrimal duct into the nose, where it can be absorbed into the blood.

test.q: Why can timolol eye drops slow the heart?
choices: It builds up in the lens over weeks
It crosses the retina into the blood
It is activated by corneal enzymes
It skips first-pass liver metabolism
test.explain: Drug absorbed through the nasal lining enters the circulation directly, avoiding first-pass metabolism in the liver, so systemic beta-blockade can occur.

test.q: Which corneal layer is the main barrier to hydrophilic drugs?
choices: Tear film
Endothelium
Epithelium
Stroma
test.explain: The lipophilic epithelium with tight junctions blocks water-loving drugs. The watery stroma is instead a barrier to very lipophilic drugs.

test.q: Latanoprost is described as a prodrug because:
choices: Tear ions thicken it on contact
Corneal esterases activate it
It is released from a punctal plug
It gels at eye temperature
test.explain: Latanoprost is an isopropyl ester that corneal esterases hydrolyze to the active acid. Gelling with temperature or ions describes in-situ gels such as poloxamers or gellan gum.

test.q: What is the main concern with benzalkonium chloride in eye drops?
choices: It speeds drug drainage into the nose
It harms the eye surface over time
It blocks drug passage across the cornea
It raises the pressure inside the eye
test.explain: BAK is an effective preservative, but chronic use damages surface epithelium, which drives demand for preservative-free products.

test.q: Why are drugs for wet macular degeneration given by intravitreal injection?
choices: Drops barely reach the retina
Pills raise pressure in the eye
Drops sting the cornea too much
Ointments blur the patient's vision
test.explain: Topical drugs are mostly lost before reaching the back of the eye, and the blood-retinal barrier limits systemic delivery, so injection into the vitreous is used.

test.q: Ozurdex is best described as:
choices: A nonbiodegradable fluocinolone implant
An anti-VEGF antibody fragment
A biodegradable dexamethasone implant
A refillable ranibizumab port
test.explain: Ozurdex is dexamethasone in a biodegradable PLGA implant. Iluvien is the non-biodegradable fluocinolone implant.

test.q: The barrier that limits entry of systemic drugs into the back of the eye is formed by:
choices: Lens capsule and ciliary body
Retinal vessels and the RPE
Corneal epithelium and stroma
The conjunctiva and the sclera
test.explain: The blood-retinal barrier consists of the retinal capillary endothelium (inner) and the retinal pigment epithelium (outer).

test.q: Pressing on the inner corner of the eye after a drop, called punctal ___, reduces systemic absorption.
test.explain: Punctal occlusion slows drainage into the nasolacrimal duct, keeping drug on the eye and out of the bloodstream.

test.q: What is the name of the gel-filled cavity at the back of the eye where anti-VEGF drugs are injected?
test.explain: Intravitreal injections deliver drug through the pars plana into the vitreous, next to the retina.

test.q: Multidose eye drop bottles contain ___ to stop microbial growth after opening.
test.explain: Preservatives such as benzalkonium chloride keep multidose bottles from becoming contaminated.

kidTest.q: What do tears and blinking do to an eye drop?
choices: Make it much stronger
Wash most of it away
Turn it into a crystal
kidTest.explain: Like windshield wipers, blinking and tears wash much of the drop away.

kidTest.q: Why do some people taste their eye drops?
choices: The drop dries and floats in the air
The drop soaks through the cheek
The drop drains down into the nose
kidTest.explain: A tiny tube carries extra drops from the eye into the nose, and the nose connects to the throat.

kidTest.q: How does a tiny eye insert work?
choices: It cleans the tears quickly
It helps the eye see farther
It lets medicine out slowly
kidTest.explain: Like a tea bag, an insert lets medicine out a little at a time.

kidTest.q: How can an eye doctor get medicine to the very back of the eye?
choices: With a very thin needle
With lots of extra drops
With a warm cloth on the eye
kidTest.explain: After numbing the eye, the doctor uses a very thin needle to place medicine right inside.

kidTest.q: Eye medicine must be super clean with no germs. The grown-up word is s _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Sterile means free of germs, which keeps the eye safe from infection.

advancedTest.q: Why does vitreous half-life generally increase from small molecules to full antibodies?
choices: Large molecules exit mainly via aqueous outflow, not across RPE
Small molecules are rapidly broken down by vitreous enzymes
Large molecules bind collagen and stay trapped in the gel
Large molecules are pumped back into the vitreous by RPE
advancedTest.explain: Small lipophilic drugs can also leave by the posterior route across retina and RPE. Large hydrophilic molecules depend on slower anterior clearance with aqueous turnover. Most molecules diffuse fairly freely through the gel, so trapping is not the explanation.

advancedTest.q: Why might a small fragment like brolucizumab be chosen despite faster clearance per molecule?
choices: It crosses the cornea well enough to use as drops
It recruits FcRn to recycle within the retina
It is less likely to provoke immune reactions
More binding sites fit in one injection volume
advancedTest.explain: At about 26 kDa, more molecules fit into the same injected volume, raising molar concentration. In practice, brolucizumab was linked to immune-mediated retinal vasculitis, and it lacks an Fc region for FcRn binding.

advancedTest.q: Intravitreal bevacizumab suppresses plasma VEGF longer than ranibizumab mainly because:
choices: It lacks an Fc region, which slows kidney clearance
It binds VEGF through irreversible covalent bonds
Its Fc region allows FcRn-mediated recycling
It escapes the eye faster via the nasolacrimal duct
advancedTest.explain: Full-length IgG bevacizumab is rescued from degradation by FcRn, prolonging systemic exposure. Ranibizumab is an Fab without Fc, so it clears quickly from the blood.

advancedTest.q: If a manufacturer makes an eye drop smaller while keeping drug concentration the same, what is expected?
choices: Ocular effect falls in direct proportion to volume
Systemic exposure rises because drainage speeds up
Corneal absorption stops because the tear film dries
Ocular effect is largely kept; systemic spillover falls
advancedTest.explain: Drainage rate rises with instilled volume, so the excess in a large drop is mostly lost to the nose and the blood. A smaller drop keeps much of the corneal delivery while reducing nasolacrimal spillover.

lessons.title: Parenteral Routes and Long-Acting Depot Injectables

levels.kid:
Some medicines can't be swallowed. The tummy would break them down, or they need to work very fast. So doctors give them as a shot. Skipping the gut like this is called a **parenteral** route.

A shot can go to different places:
- Into a **vein**, so medicine reaches the blood right away.
- Into a **muscle**, like the top of your arm.
- Just **under the skin**, into a soft fatty layer.

Some special shots are called **depots**. A depot is like a tiny hidden pantry of medicine. It sits in the muscle or under the skin and lets out a little bit at a time, for weeks or even months. That way a person doesn't have to remember a pill every single day.
levels.hs:
**Parenteral** literally means "beside the gut." In practice it means giving a drug by injection or infusion, so it skips the digestive system and the liver's first-pass metabolism. Because a needle breaks the skin barrier, parenteral products must be **sterile** (free of microbes) and free of fever-causing bacterial fragments called pyrogens.

The main routes:
- **Intravenous (IV)**: straight into a vein. All of the drug reaches the bloodstream, so bioavailability is 100% and the effect is fastest.
- **Intramuscular (IM)**: into a muscle such as the deltoid (shoulder) or the gluteal (hip) muscles. Muscle has a rich blood supply, so absorption takes minutes to hours.
- **Subcutaneous (SC)**: into the fat under the skin, used for insulin and many antibody drugs. Absorption is usually slower and steadier.
- **Intradermal (ID)**: into the skin itself, used for the tuberculosis skin test.

A **long-acting injectable (LAI)**, or **depot**, is a formulation designed to sit at the injection site and release drug slowly for weeks to months. A real example is **haloperidol decanoate**, an antipsychotic dissolved in sesame oil and injected into muscle, where it releases drug for about a month. For people with schizophrenia, who may struggle to take daily pills, one injection can replace many tablets and help prevent relapse.

The trade-off: once a depot is injected, it is hard to withdraw quickly if side effects appear.
levels.college:
Parenteral administration bypasses gastrointestinal degradation and hepatic first-pass metabolism. Since the skin barrier is breached, products must be sterile, essentially endotoxin-free, and ideally near-isotonic and near-physiological pH.

**Absorption from IM and SC sites.** IV injection has no absorption step. From muscle or fat, drug diffuses through interstitial fluid into capillaries; small lipophilic molecules cross capillary walls readily, while large proteins (roughly above 16 kDa) drain mainly via **lymphatics**, which is slower. Local blood flow sets the pace: among IM sites, absorption is generally **deltoid > vastus lateralis > gluteal**. The **ventrogluteal** site is preferred over the dorsogluteal because it lies away from the sciatic nerve. SC volumes are traditionally small; co-formulated **hyaluronidase** temporarily breaks down hyaluronan in the tissue matrix so larger volumes can be given, enabling SC versions of antibodies like trastuzumab and daratumumab.

**Depot strategies.** A long-acting injectable makes release from the site, not elimination, the rate-limiting step:
- **Oil solutions of ester prodrugs**: haloperidol or fluphenazine decanoate in sesame oil. The long fatty ester makes the drug highly lipophilic, so it partitions slowly out of the oil into tissue fluid, where esterases free the active drug. The **Z-track** technique prevents leakage back along the needle path.
- **Aqueous nanocrystal suspensions**: paliperidone palmitate, aripiprazole lauroxil, cabotegravir. Poorly soluble crystals dissolve slowly; crystal size sets the rate.
- **Biodegradable microspheres** of **PLGA** (poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid)): leuprolide (Lupron Depot), risperidone (Risperdal Consta), octreotide (Sandostatin LAR), exenatide (Bydureon). Water hydrolyzes the polymer's ester bonds, releasing drug.
- **In situ forming implants**: PLGA dissolved in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone precipitates into a solid depot on contact with tissue water (Eligard).

**Flip-flop kinetics.** When absorption is much slower than elimination (ka << ke), the terminal decline in plasma levels reflects absorption, so the apparent half-life belongs to the depot, not the drug.
levels.phd:
PLGA microsphere release is classically **triphasic**: an initial **burst** from surface-associated and pore-accessible drug; a **lag** while the polymer hydrates and chains are cleaved with little mass loss; then **erosion-controlled release** once oligomers become water-soluble. PLGA undergoes **bulk erosion** because water penetrates faster than ester bonds hydrolyze, so degradation occurs throughout the matrix. Carboxylic acid end groups and lactic/glycolic acid products catalyze further hydrolysis (**autocatalysis**), and the microclimate pH inside particles can fall well below 4. This can denature proteins or **acylate** peptides at lysine amines and the N-terminus, a documented problem for octreotide and leuprolide.

Release is tuned by the **lactide:glycolide ratio** (lactide's methyl group adds hydrophobicity, so higher lactide content degrades more slowly; 50:50 degrades fastest), molecular weight, acid versus ester end caps, and particle size. Manufacturing uses water-in-oil-in-water double emulsion with solvent evaporation, spray drying, or coacervation. Lupron Depot (Takeda, approved 1989) pioneered the field. The lag has clinical consequences: Risperdal Consta releases little risperidone for about three weeks, so oral overlap was needed at initiation.

**Nanocrystal suspensions** exploit the Noyes–Whitney relation: dissolution rate scales with surface area and saturation solubility. A prodrug with extremely low aqueous solubility plus a controlled particle size distribution sets the release rate; larger crystals mean less surface area and a longer apparent half-life. Stabilizers such as polysorbate 20 or poloxamers prevent aggregation and **Ostwald ripening** (large crystals growing at the expense of small ones), which would drift the release profile in storage. Rat studies by Darville and colleagues showed IM paliperidone palmitate depots become infiltrated by macrophages that engulf crystals, so the host response contributes to release.

**Flip-flop pharmacokinetics.** In a one-compartment model with first-order absorption, when ka << k the terminal slope approximates ka. Time to steady state then depends on the absorption half-life, which can be months, so loading strategies such as initiation injections into the faster-absorbing deltoid are used.

Evidence is nuanced. Tiihonen's Finnish nationwide cohorts linked LAIs to substantially lower rehospitalization than the same drugs taken orally, while early RCT meta-analyses (Kishimoto 2014) found little difference. A plausible explanation: RCTs enroll adherent volunteers, blunting the adherence advantage that LAIs offer.
levels.expert:
LAIs now extend well beyond psychiatry. In HIV, **cabotegravir/rilpivirine** (Cabenuva, 2021) provides injectable maintenance therapy, and **cabotegravir** alone (Apretude) proved superior to daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine for PrEP in HPTN 083 (cisgender men and transgender women) and HPTN 084 (cisgender women), largely by eliminating adherence failure. **Lenacapavir**, a capsid inhibitor potent and insoluble enough to form a SC depot lasting about six months, yielded zero infections among women in PURPOSE 1 (2024) and very few in PURPOSE 2. It was approved for PrEP (Yeztugo) in 2025, and once-yearly IM formulations are in trials.

Clinical pitfalls:
- **The pharmacokinetic tail.** After the last cabotegravir injection, concentrations decline over a year or more. If HIV is acquired in that window, sub-suppressive levels can select integrase resistance, so guidelines advise covering the tail with oral PrEP if risk continues. Breakthrough infections on cabotegravir show delayed, blunted antibody responses, so HIV RNA testing is recommended.
- **Failure predictors.** For cabotegravir/rilpivirine, BMI ≥30, HIV-1 subtype A6/A1 and archived rilpivirine resistance mutations predict virologic failure; low troughs in obesity likely contribute.
- **Technique and body habitus.** In obesity a standard needle may deposit intended IM drug into fat, changing absorption. Needle length and site choice matter.
- **Rare, irreversible reactions.** Olanzapine pamoate can cause **post-injection delirium/sedation syndrome** in roughly 0.07% of injections, probably from inadvertent vascular entry and rapid dissolution, so a 3-hour post-injection observation and a REMS program are required. Testosterone undecanoate in oil can cause pulmonary oil microembolism (POME).

In oncology, hyaluronidase-co-formulated SC antibodies (daratumumab, the pertuzumab/trastuzumab combination Phesgo) cut chair time from hours to minutes, which patients prefer and clinics value.

In psychiatry, the PRIDE trial (Alphs, 2015) showed paliperidone palmitate delayed treatment failure versus oral antipsychotics in people with schizophrenia and justice involvement. Clinicians must also counter the perception that LAIs are coercive; shared decision-making improves uptake.

Open problems: proving generic equivalence for complex injectables (PLGA microspheres need matching polymer composition plus discriminating in vitro release tests, and in vitro–in vivo correlation for accelerated assays remains an active FDA research area), and designing depots that can be retrieved if needed.

keyPoints: Parenteral routes (IV, IM, SC, ID) bypass the gut and first-pass metabolism
IV gives 100% bioavailability; IM and SC absorption depend on blood flow and molecule size
Depots make release from the site, not elimination, the rate-limiting step
Main depot types: oil ester prodrugs, nanocrystal suspensions, PLGA microspheres, in situ implants
Flip-flop kinetics: the terminal half-life reflects slow absorption from the depot
LAIs improve adherence but are hard to reverse and leave a long drug tail

test.q: In pharmaceutics, 'parenteral' usually refers to drugs given by:
choices: An injection
An inhaled mist
A rectal suppository
A swallowed pill
test.explain: Parenteral means bypassing the gut, and in practice it means injection or infusion. Suppositories and pills use the digestive tract; inhalers are their own route.

test.q: Which route gives 100% bioavailability by definition?
choices: Intramuscular
Intravenous
Intradermal
Subcutaneous
test.explain: IV places the drug directly into the bloodstream, so there is no absorption step. IM, SC and ID all require absorption from tissue.

test.q: Which site is preferred for gluteal injections because it lies away from the sciatic nerve?
choices: Deltoid
Dorsogluteal
Vastus lateralis
Ventrogluteal
test.explain: The ventrogluteal site avoids the sciatic nerve, which runs near the dorsogluteal site. Deltoid and vastus lateralis are not gluteal sites.

test.q: In flip-flop kinetics, typical of depot injections, the terminal half-life mainly reflects:
choices: The rate kidneys clear it
The rate it is absorbed
The rate it binds plasma proteins
The rate the liver breaks it down
test.explain: When absorption is much slower than elimination, the slow release from the injection site controls how fast levels fall, so the apparent half-life belongs to the depot.

test.q: Why is haloperidol made into a decanoate ester for its oil depot?
choices: To make it water-soluble for IV
To speed its dissolving in blood
To slow its exit from the oil
To block its breakdown in the liver
test.explain: The long fatty ester makes the drug highly lipophilic, so it partitions slowly from the oil into tissue fluid, where esterases free the active drug.

test.q: How do PLGA microspheres mainly release their drug?
choices: Water slowly splits the polymer
Spheres melt at body temperature
Enzymes digest the drug first
An osmotic core pumps drug out
test.explain: PLGA's ester bonds are hydrolyzed by water, so the polymer degrades and releases the drug over weeks. Osmotic pumps are a different technology.

test.q: Among common IM sites, absorption is usually fastest from the:
choices: Deltoid muscle
Calf muscle
Thigh muscle
Gluteal muscle
test.explain: Absorption follows blood flow: deltoid is generally faster than vastus lateralis (thigh), which is faster than gluteal.

test.q: Paliperidone palmitate long-acting injection is formulated as:
choices: A gel that forms in tissue
Aqueous drug nanocrystals
A solution in sesame oil
Biodegradable microspheres
test.explain: Paliperidone palmitate is a poorly soluble prodrug given as an aqueous nanocrystal suspension; slow crystal dissolution sets the release rate.

test.q: A major drawback of a long-acting depot compared with daily pills is that it:
choices: Undergoes more first-pass loss
Is hard to withdraw quickly
Gives higher peak-to-trough swings
Adds to the daily pill burden
test.explain: Once injected, the depot keeps releasing drug, so side effects can't be stopped quickly. Depots actually reduce pill burden and smooth out concentration swings.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for the biodegradable lactide-glycolide copolymer used in microspheres such as Lupron Depot?
test.explain: PLGA, poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid), degrades by hydrolysis into lactic and glycolic acids.

test.q: The ___ technique displaces the skin before an IM injection so oily depots don't leak back out.
test.explain: Z-track injection creates a zig-zag needle path that seals the drug in the muscle.

test.q: Which enzyme, co-formulated with some antibody drugs, temporarily breaks down the tissue matrix so larger volumes can be injected under the skin?
test.explain: Hyaluronidase depolymerizes hyaluronan, enabling SC versions of antibodies like trastuzumab and daratumumab.

kidTest.q: What does a depot shot do?
choices: Makes medicine taste better
Cleans the skin first
Lets medicine out slowly
kidTest.explain: A depot is like a hidden pantry that releases a little medicine at a time for weeks or months.

kidTest.q: A shot into a vein sends medicine:
choices: Into the bones first
Into the tummy first
Into the blood fast
kidTest.explain: A vein is a blood tube, so the medicine reaches the blood right away.

kidTest.q: Where does an 'under the skin' shot go?
choices: Into a deep vein
Into the fatty layer
Into the bone inside
kidTest.explain: Under-the-skin shots go into the soft fatty layer just below the skin.

kidTest.q: Why are some medicines given as shots instead of swallowed?
choices: Pills are too heavy to carry
The tummy would destroy them
Shots are cheaper to make
kidTest.explain: Some medicines get broken down in the tummy, so a shot skips the gut.

kidTest.q: A slow-release shot that lasts for weeks is called a d _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A depot stores medicine at the injection site and lets it out slowly.

advancedTest.q: A person stops cabotegravir long-acting PrEP but remains at risk of HIV. Why is oral PrEP advised during the pharmacokinetic tail?
choices: The depot may release a sudden burst once dosing ends
Cabotegravir induces its own metabolism after dosing ends
Oral drug is needed to clear leftover crystals from muscle
Low lingering levels could select for resistance
advancedTest.explain: Concentrations fall slowly over a year or more. If HIV is acquired while levels are sub-suppressive, integrase resistance can be selected; oral PrEP keeps protection adequate.

advancedTest.q: Why did risperidone PLGA microspheres (Risperdal Consta) need oral overlap for about three weeks after the first injection?
choices: The drug is poorly absorbed from the deltoid muscle
Risperidone needs activation by the liver first
Little drug is released until the polymer erodes
The microspheres first release an excessive burst
advancedTest.explain: PLGA release is triphasic, and the lag phase (hydration and chain scission without mass loss) releases little drug before erosion-controlled release begins.

advancedTest.q: For an aqueous nanocrystal depot showing flip-flop kinetics, increasing the median crystal size would most likely:
choices: Lengthen the apparent terminal half-life of the drug
Have no effect, since clearance controls the terminal phase
Shorten the elimination half-life set by the kidneys
Raise the initial peak and shorten the apparent half-life
advancedTest.explain: By Noyes–Whitney, larger crystals have less surface area and dissolve more slowly. In flip-flop kinetics absorption controls the terminal phase, so the apparent half-life lengthens.

advancedTest.q: Changing a PLGA microsphere from 50:50 to 75:25 lactide:glycolide would be expected to:
choices: Convert bulk erosion into purely surface erosion
Speed degradation, because lactide hydrolyzes faster than glycolide
Abolish the initial burst, because surface drug is removed
Slow degradation, as lactide's methyl group adds hydrophobicity
advancedTest.explain: Higher lactide content makes the polymer more hydrophobic, slowing water uptake and hydrolysis; 50:50 degrades fastest. PLGA still erodes in bulk, and the burst depends on surface drug, not the monomer ratio.

lessons.title: Implants, Infusion Pumps and Intrathecal Delivery

levels.kid:
Most medicines are swallowed or given as a shot. But some people need medicine every day for months or even years. For them, doctors use clever helpers.

An **implant** is a tiny rod or wafer placed under the skin. It lets out medicine slowly, a little bit each day, like a wet sponge slowly dripping.

A **pump** is a small machine, about the size of a hockey puck. It can sit outside the body, or inside, under the skin of the belly. It pushes out tiny drops of medicine on a schedule.

Some pumps send medicine straight into the fluid around the spinal cord. That is called **intrathecal** delivery. The medicine skips the long trip through the body and goes right where it is needed, so a very small amount works.
levels.hs:
Some medicines must be given steadily for months or years, or must reach places that pills and ordinary shots reach poorly. Three tools solve these problems.

**Implants** are small solid devices placed under the skin that release drug slowly. A real example is **Nexplanon**, a flexible rod about 4 cm long inserted under the skin of the upper arm. It releases the hormone etonogestrel to prevent pregnancy for up to 3 years. Some implants are **biodegradable**, meaning they break down in the body; others must be removed.

**Infusion pumps** push liquid drug at a controlled rate. External insulin pumps deliver insulin through a thin tube under the skin, and **automated insulin delivery** systems link the pump to a continuous glucose monitor so the device can adjust insulin by itself. Implanted pumps sit under the skin of the abdomen and are refilled with a needle through the skin.

**Intrathecal** delivery puts drug directly into the **cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)**, the clear liquid bathing the brain and spinal cord. This bypasses the **blood-brain barrier**, the tight lining of blood-vessel cells that keeps many drugs out of the nervous system.

Example: **baclofen** treats severe muscle stiffness (spasticity) from cerebral palsy, multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injury. Swallowed baclofen crosses into the spinal cord poorly, so effective oral treatment often causes drowsiness. Given intrathecally by a pump, a tiny amount works right at the spinal cord.
levels.college:
Implants, pumps and intrathecal systems share three goals: steady drug levels, fewer administrations, and delivery to sites that systemic dosing reaches poorly.

**Implant release mechanisms**
- **Reservoir** implants hold drug inside a rate-controlling membrane. While the core stays saturated, release is nearly constant (**zero-order**).
- **Matrix** implants disperse drug throughout a polymer. Drug near the surface leaves first, so the diffusion path lengthens and cumulative release grows in proportion to the square root of time (the **Higuchi** model).
- **Biodegradable** implants erode in the body, so no removal is needed. Examples include PLGA implants such as Zoladex (goserelin) for prostate cancer, and **Gliadel** wafers, which release the chemotherapy drug **carmustine** into the cavity left after brain tumor surgery.

**Pump types**
- **External**: insulin pumps, patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pumps, disposable elastomeric balloon pumps.
- **Implanted programmable** (e.g., Medtronic SynchroMed II): a battery-powered peristaltic mechanism; the rate is changed wirelessly with a programmer.
- **Constant-flow**: a gas propellant pressurizes the reservoir and a narrow capillary sets a fixed flow. To change the delivered amount, clinicians refill the pump with a different drug concentration.
- **Osmotic** (e.g., DUROS technology): water drawn in by an osmotic agent pushes a piston at a steady rate.

**Intrathecal delivery**
Adults have about 150 mL of CSF and produce roughly 500 mL a day, so CSF turns over several times daily. A catheter is placed in the lumbar intrathecal space and tunneled under the skin to a pump in the abdominal wall. Patients usually first receive a **trial dose by lumbar puncture** to confirm benefit. In the US, drugs approved for chronic intrathecal pump infusion are **morphine**, **ziconotide** and **baclofen**.

Related routes: an **Ommaya reservoir**, a dome under the scalp connected to a catheter in a lateral ventricle, allows repeated chemotherapy (methotrexate, cytarabine) into the ventricles. The antisense drug **nusinersen** for spinal muscular atrophy is given by repeated lumbar puncture.
levels.phd:
**Polymer erosion.** PLGA degrades by hydrolysis of ester bonds throughout its bulk (**bulk erosion**). Water penetrates faster than chains break, and acidic lactic and glycolic oligomers trapped inside autocatalyze further hydrolysis, so the core can degrade faster than the surface and release often shows a late burst. The lactide:glycolide ratio tunes degradation; 50:50 copolymers, being amorphous, degrade fastest. Hydrophobic **polyanhydrides** instead undergo **surface erosion**, thinning layer by layer like a bar of soap and giving more predictable release. Langer and Brem exploited this in Gliadel (carmustine in polifeprosan 20). In Westphal's 2003 phase III trial in newly diagnosed malignant glioma, median survival was 13.9 versus 11.6 months with placebo wafers. A limitation: carmustine penetrates only millimetres into brain before capillary uptake clears it, a classic diffusion-elimination trade-off.

**Osmotic pumps.** Output is set by membrane water permeability, area and thickness and the osmotic pressure difference. While the osmotic agent remains saturated, the gradient is constant and delivery is zero-order (the logic of Theeuwes's elementary osmotic pump).

**Constant-flow pumps.** A vapour propellant drives flow, and its pressure rises with temperature; the pressure difference also grows when ambient pressure falls. Fever or high altitude therefore increases flow, which matters for narrow-margin drugs.

**Intrathecal pharmacokinetics.** CSF is not a well-stirred compartment. Slow infusion produces a steep concentration gradient around the catheter tip with limited spread (Bernards and colleagues). Lipid solubility governs fate: **hydrophilic morphine** has long CSF residence and spreads rostrally, explaining delayed respiratory depression hours after a bolus; **lipophilic fentanyl and sufentanil** leave CSF quickly into epidural fat and blood and act more segmentally. Conventional conversion tables treat intrathecal morphine as roughly 300 times as potent as oral.

**Ziconotide** is synthetic omega-conotoxin MVIIA from the cone snail Conus magus. It blocks N-type (CaV2.2) calcium channels on primary afferent terminals in the dorsal horn, reducing glutamate and substance P release. As a 25-amino-acid peptide it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier. It causes no opioid-type tolerance or withdrawal, but a narrow therapeutic window and a boxed warning for psychiatric and neurological effects demand slow titration.
levels.expert:
**Intrathecal pump safety in practice**
- **Catheter-tip inflammatory mass (granuloma)**: a sterile mass at the catheter tip, linked mainly to high concentrations of opioids such as morphine and hydromorphone at low flow. The typical story is gradually failing analgesia, then new radicular pain or progressive weakness from cord compression. Contrast MRI confirms it; stopping infusion through that catheter often shrinks it, but some patients need surgical decompression.
- **Baclofen withdrawal**: abrupt interruption (catheter kink or disconnection, empty reservoir, battery end of life, refill error) causes rebound spasticity, itching, high fever, altered mental state and, at worst, rhabdomyolysis, multiorgan failure and death. Treatment is rapid restoration of intrathecal baclofen; oral baclofen and benzodiazepines are only a bridge.
- **Pocket fill**: injecting a refill into the subcutaneous pocket instead of the reservoir can cause massive overdose. Templates, aspiration checks and ultrasound or fluoroscopic guidance reduce risk.
- **MRI**: the magnetic field can temporarily stall a programmable pump's rotor, so the pump is interrogated after the scan.

The Polyanalgesic Consensus Conference guidelines rank ziconotide and morphine as first-line intrathecal agents and support considering intrathecal therapy earlier in cancer pain.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Gliadel needs a resection cavity and can cause seizures, cerebral oedema, CSF leak and poor wound healing; wafer-related changes can mimic tumor on early postoperative MRI. Intrathecal antisense therapy has expanded: after nusinersen (2016), **tofersen** for SOD1-ALS received accelerated FDA approval in 2023, making lumbar puncture a routine route in genetic neurology.

**Implant advances and pitfalls.** Nexplanon contains barium sulfate so it shows on X-ray; reports of deep insertion, nerve injury and migration led to revised insertion-site guidance. Wirelessly programmable microchip implants (Farra and colleagues, 2012) delivered teriparatide in women with osteoporosis. The ITCA 650 osmotic mini-pump for exenatide failed to win FDA approval, a reminder that device reliability is judged as strictly as the drug. Long-acting implants for HIV prevention are in trials.

**Automated insulin delivery** has moved from the first hybrid closed-loop system (2016) to systems initialized with body weight alone. Open questions: preventing catheter failure, predicting individual CSF distribution, and reaching brain parenchyma rather than CSF.

keyPoints: Implants release drug slowly from under the skin for months to years
Reservoir implants give near zero-order release; matrix release falls with the square root of time
Pumps can be external, implanted programmable, gas-driven constant-flow or osmotic
Intrathecal delivery puts drug into CSF, bypassing the blood-brain barrier
Morphine, ziconotide and baclofen are approved for chronic intrathecal pump infusion in the US
Key pump hazards: catheter-tip granuloma, baclofen withdrawal and pocket fill errors

test.q: Why is baclofen for severe spasticity often given intrathecally?
choices: It avoids breakdown by stomach acid
It speeds absorption from the gut
It acts directly on skeletal muscle
It bypasses the blood-brain barrier
test.explain: Swallowed baclofen crosses into the spinal cord poorly. Intrathecal delivery puts it straight into the CSF, so a tiny amount acts at the cord with less drowsiness.

test.q: A reservoir implant with a rate-controlling membrane and a saturated core gives what kind of release?
choices: One large burst followed by little release
Nearly constant, zero-order release
Release falling with the square root of time
Release that steadily rises over time
test.explain: While the core stays saturated, the membrane sets a steady rate, giving zero-order release. Square-root-of-time decline is typical of matrix systems.

test.q: Where is the Nexplanon contraceptive rod placed?
choices: Inside the uterine cavity
Under the skin of the upper arm
Into a vein of the forearm
Into the fluid around the spinal cord
test.explain: Nexplanon is a 4 cm rod inserted under the skin of the upper arm, releasing etonogestrel for up to 3 years.

test.q: With a gas-driven constant-flow pump, how do clinicians change the amount of drug delivered?
choices: Refilling with a different concentration
Raising the voltage supplied by its battery
Reprogramming its motor with a wireless tablet
Replacing the catheter with a wider one
test.explain: The capillary fixes the flow rate, so the only practical lever is the drug concentration in the reservoir. Wireless reprogramming applies to programmable pumps.

test.q: About how much cerebrospinal fluid does an adult have at any one time?
choices: About 1.5 L
About 50 mL
About 150 mL
About 500 mL
test.explain: Adults hold about 150 mL of CSF. Roughly 500 mL is produced per day, which is the tempting wrong answer.

test.q: An Ommaya reservoir is mainly used for:
choices: Giving chemotherapy into the ventricles
Releasing hormone into the upper arm
Draining extra CSF into the abdomen
Holding insulin under the belly skin
test.explain: An Ommaya reservoir is a dome under the scalp connected to a ventricular catheter, used for repeated chemotherapy such as methotrexate. Draining CSF is the job of a shunt.

test.q: Before a permanent intrathecal pump is implanted, patients usually receive:
choices: A test infusion through a vein
A trial dose by lumbar puncture
A short course of oral steroids
A contrast scan of the abdomen
